question: What are the three types of dependency injection in Spring?
title: Three Types of Dependency Injection in Spring
direct_answer: The three DI types are: **Constructor injection** (dependencies via constructor — recommended), **Setter injection** (via setter methods — for optional dependencies), and **Field injection** (`@Autowired` directly on field — convenient but discouraged in production code).

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of all three DI types and their tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing field injection because it's the simplest to write
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clearly state constructor injection is recommended and explain why

sections.title: Three Ways Spring Injects Dependencies
sections.content: Spring Framework gives you three ways to inject dependencies into your beans: **constructor injection**, **setter injection**, and **field injection**. Think of dependency injection as Spring's way of handing your class the objects it needs to do its job — like a waiter bringing ingredients to a chef. **Constructor injection** passes dependencies through the class constructor, making them required and immutable. **Setter injection** uses setter methods to inject dependencies after object creation, allowing optional dependencies. **Field injection** uses `@Autowired` directly on fields, letting Spring set them via reflection — the shortest code but the weakest approach. Most production Spring Boot apps use constructor injection as the default because it makes dependencies explicit, enables immutability with `final` fields, and simplifies testing. Setter injection handles optional dependencies gracefully. Field injection is convenient for quick prototypes but creates testing headaches and hides dependency requirements.

sections.title: All Three Injection Types in Action
Key Points
content: **Constructor injection**: Dependencies passed via constructor, can be marked final, recommended for required dependencies
**Setter injection**: Dependencies set via setter methods after object creation, ideal for optional dependencies with @Autowired(required=false)
**Field injection**: @Autowired directly on field, shortest syntax but discouraged because it breaks immutability and complicates testing
**Immutability**: Only constructor injection allows final fields, preventing accidental reassignment after initialization
**Explicitness**: Constructor shows all required dependencies in one place; field injection hides them inside the class body
**Testability**: Constructor injection lets you new MyService(mockRepo) in unit tests; field injection requires Spring context or reflection
**Modern Spring Boot**: Since Spring 4.3, single-constructor classes don't need @Autowired annotation

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring supports three dependency injection types: constructor, setter, and field injection. Constructor injection passes dependencies through the class constructor. It's the recommended approach because you can make fields final, which prevents accidental changes. All required dependencies show up clearly in the constructor signature. You can also test the class without Spring by just calling new OrderService with a mock repository. Setter injection uses setter methods to inject dependencies after the object is created. It's perfect for optional dependencies. You mark the setter with at-Autowired required equals false, and Spring injects the bean if it exists. If not, the field stays null and your class still works. Field injection puts at-Autowired directly on the field. Spring uses reflection to set it. It's the shortest code, but most teams avoid it in production. You can't make the field final, and you can't easily pass a mock in tests without starting the entire Spring context. The common mistake freshers make is using field injection everywhere because it's fewer lines. In real Spring Boot projects, you'll see constructor injection as the standard. One tip: since Spring 4.3, if your class has only one constructor, you don't even need the at-Autowired annotation. Spring figures it out automatically.

beats.text: Spring supports three injection styles. Constructor injection: dependencies are parameters of the constructor. Spring creates the bean by calling the constructor with the required beans. Setter injection: @Autowired on a setter method — Spring calls the setter after creating the object. Field injection: @Autowired directly on a private field — Spring sets it via reflection after construction.

Different situations call for different injection styles. Required dependencies belong in the constructor — they're explicit and immutable. Optional dependencies fit setters — the class works without them. Field injection exists for convenience, but it sacrifices testability and immutability.

items: Constructor injection: fields can be final. Works in tests with plain new. Spring 4.3+ doesn't require @Autowired if there's only one constructor. Recommended for all required dependencies.
Setter injection: @Autowired(required=false) on the setter. Class initializes even if the dependency is absent. Good for optional behavior like caching or metrics.
Field injection: @Autowired on a private field. Zero boilerplate. But fields can't be final, testing needs Spring or reflection hacks, and circular deps may not fail at startup.

items: Don't use field injection in production code — you can't make fields final, dependencies are hidden, and tests need Spring or reflection.
Don't use constructor injection for optional dependencies — if the bean is absent, Spring throws at startup. Use setter injection with required=false instead.

question: Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection in Spring?
title: Constructor Injection vs Field Injection — Why Constructor Wins
direct_answer: **Constructor injection is preferred** because: dependencies can be `final` (immutable), all required deps are explicit in the constructor signature, the class can be tested without Spring (pass mocks directly), and Spring detects circular dependencies at startup rather than hiding them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of production code quality concerns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying field injection is fine because it's less verbose
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all four reasons: immutability, explicitness, testability, fail-fast circular dep detection

sections.title: Why Constructor Injection Wins in Production Code
sections.content: Constructor injection is the preferred DI approach in professional Spring Boot applications because it solves four critical problems that field injection creates. **Immutability**: constructor-injected dependencies can be `final`, preventing accidental reassignment after initialization. **Explicitness**: every required dependency appears in the constructor signature, making the class's needs obvious at a glance. **Testability**: you can instantiate the class with `new MyService(mockRepo)` in unit tests without starting Spring's application context. **Fail-fast behavior**: circular dependencies cause Spring to throw an exception at startup with constructor injection, rather than hiding the problem until runtime. Field injection using `@Autowired` directly on fields looks cleaner with less boilerplate, but it trades short-term convenience for long-term maintainability issues.

sections.title: When Each Injection Type Makes Sense
sections.content: **Use constructor injection** for all required dependencies in production code. If your service needs a repository to function, inject it through the constructor and mark the field `final`. This is the Spring Boot community standard and what you'll see in most enterprise codebases. Modern tools like Lombok's `@RequiredArgsConstructor` eliminate the boilerplate by auto-generating the constructor for all `final` fields. **Use field injection** only for quick prototypes, spike solutions, or learning exercises where testability doesn't matter. Some legacy Spring applications still use field injection everywhere, but new code should avoid it. The five lines saved per class aren't worth the testing complexity. If you're writing code that will be maintained beyond next week, constructor injection is the pragmatic choice.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Immutability guarantee**: Constructor injection allows final fields, making dependencies unchangeable after initialization
**Explicit dependencies**: Constructor signature shows all required dependencies at a glance, improving code readability
**Pure unit testing**: With constructor injection you can write tests using new MyService without Spring context or mocking frameworks
**Circular dependency detection**: Constructor injection fails fast at application startup; field injection fails later during runtime when the bean is first used
**Production standard**: Constructor injection is the recommended practice in Spring Boot documentation and enterprise codebases
**Lombok integration**: @RequiredArgsConstructor generates the constructor for all final fields, eliminating boilerplate
**Testability cost**: Field injection requires @SpringBootTest or ReflectionTestUtils.setField for testing, slowing down test suites significantly

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Constructor injection is preferred over field injection for four main reasons. First, immutability. With constructor injection, you can mark dependencies as final. Once they're set in the constructor, they can't be changed. That prevents bugs where someone accidentally reassigns a critical dependency. Second, explicitness. When you look at a constructor, you immediately see every dependency the class needs. With field injection, you have to scan through the entire class to find all the at-Autowired annotations. Third, testability. Constructor injection lets you write pure unit tests. You just call new OrderService with a mock repository. No Spring context needed. With field injection, you either have to start the entire Spring Boot app using at-SpringBootTest, which is slow, or you use reflection hacks like ReflectionTestUtils dot setField. Both approaches make your tests more complicated and slower. Fourth, fail-fast circular dependencies. If two beans depend on each other through constructors, Spring detects it immediately when the app starts and throws an exception. With field injection, the app starts fine, but you get a runtime error later when someone actually uses those beans. The common mistake is thinking field injection is fine because it's fewer lines of code. In a real project with hundreds of services, the testing pain adds up fast. Constructor injection is the standard in professional Spring Boot code.

question: When would you use setter injection in Spring?
title: When to Use Setter Injection in Spring
direct_answer: Use **setter injection** for **optional dependencies** — ones that aren't required for the class to function. With `@Autowired(required=false)` on the setter, Spring injects the dependency if a bean exists; otherwise the field remains null and the class still initializes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Nuanced understanding of when each injection type is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying setter injection is never useful
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a real-world optional dependency example

sections.title: The Optional Dependency Use Case
sections.content: Setter injection solves the problem of **optional dependencies** — beans that enhance functionality but aren't strictly required for the class to work. Think of a `NotificationService` that can send emails if an `EmailClient` bean is configured, but can still function without it by logging notifications instead. With **constructor injection**, every parameter is required; if the `EmailClient` bean doesn't exist, Spring fails to create the `NotificationService`. With **setter injection and `@Autowired(required=false)`**, Spring injects the `EmailClient` if it's available, but initializes `NotificationService` successfully even if it's not. This pattern is common in cross-cutting concerns like caching, metrics collection, and feature toggles where the core business logic should work regardless of whether the enhancement is available.

sections.title: Step 1: Identify Truly Optional Dependencies
sections.content: Not every dependency should be optional — most are required. Use setter injection only when the class has a meaningful fallback behavior without the dependency. For example, a `PaymentService` that logs to `AuditLogger` if available but can still process payments without it. Or a `ReportGenerator` that uses a `CacheService` to speed up repeated queries but can generate reports by querying the database directly if caching isn't configured. The key question: Can this class fulfill its core responsibility without this dependency? If the answer is no, use constructor injection to make that requirement explicit and fail fast if the dependency is missing.

sections.title: Step 2: Implement Graceful Degradation
sections.content: When you use setter injection for an optional dependency, you must handle the null case in your business logic. Typically this means checking if the field is null before using it, or providing a default implementation. For example, if `emailClient` is null, log the notification to a file instead of sending an email. Or if `cacheService` is null, skip caching and query the database directly. The pattern is: check for null, use the enhanced path if available, fall back to the basic implementation otherwise. This explicit null-checking is actually an advantage — it forces you to think about the degraded behavior. With constructor injection, you can't compile without providing every dependency.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Optional dependency definition**: A dependency that enhances functionality but isn't required for the class to fulfill its core responsibility
**@Autowired(required=false)**: Annotation on setter methods telling Spring to inject the bean if it exists, skip injection if not
**Graceful degradation**: Code must handle null optional dependencies by providing fallback behavior like logging instead of emailing
**Real-world examples**: Caching services, audit loggers, metrics collectors, feature flag managers, notification channels
**Constructor vs setter trade-off**: Constructor injection fails fast if dependency is missing; setter injection allows the bean to initialize
**Null safety**: Always check if optional dependency is null before using it to avoid NullPointerException at runtime
**Conditional bean creation**: Optional dependencies often pair with @ConditionalOnProperty or @ConditionalOnClass annotations in configuration

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You'd use setter injection for optional dependencies. Those are dependencies that improve your class but aren't required for it to function. For example, imagine a NotificationService that can send emails if an EmailClient bean is configured, but if it's not available, the service just logs notifications instead. With constructor injection, every parameter is required. If you put EmailClient in the constructor and that bean doesn't exist, Spring fails to start your application. With setter injection, you mark the setter with at-Autowired required equals false. Spring injects the EmailClient if it finds a bean, but if not, the field stays null and your NotificationService still initializes successfully. Then in your code, you check if emailClient is null. If it's there, send the email. If not, log it to a file. That's called graceful degradation. Real-world examples include caching services, audit loggers, and metrics collectors. Your core business logic works without them, but they make the system better when available. The common mistake is thinking setter injection is outdated. It's not. It's just specialized for this optional dependency scenario. Most dependencies should still use constructor injection because they're required. But when you have a true optional dependency where the class can function without it, setter injection with required equals false is the right tool.

question: Can a Spring bean have multiple injection types?
title: Multiple Injection Types in a Single Spring Bean
direct_answer: **Yes**, a Spring bean can mix injection types. Typically: **constructor injection** for required dependencies and **setter injection** for optional ones. Field injection can coexist but is discouraged. The common pattern is constructor for required + setter for optional.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you must choose one injection type for the entire class
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Recommend the constructor (required) + setter (optional) combination as best practice

sections.title: Mixing Injection Types in a Single Bean
sections.content: Spring allows you to combine multiple dependency injection types in the same class, giving you fine-grained control over how each dependency is handled. The most common pattern in production code is **constructor injection for required dependencies** and **setter injection for optional dependencies**. This hybrid approach captures the best of both worlds: required dependencies are immutable, explicit, and easily testable through the constructor, while optional dependencies can be injected if available without blocking bean creation. For example, an `OrderService` might require an `OrderRepository` (constructor) but optionally use a `CacheService` (setter) if caching is enabled. You can technically mix in **field injection** as well, but doing so defeats the benefits of constructor injection, so most teams stick to the constructor-plus-setter pattern. Spring processes constructor injection first, then setter and field injection in no guaranteed order.

sections.title: Combining Constructor and Setter Injection
Key Points
content: **Hybrid injection**: A single Spring bean can use constructor, setter, and field injection simultaneously
**Best practice pattern**: Constructor injection for required dependencies marked final, setter injection for optional dependencies
**Injection order**: Spring calls constructor first, then processes setter and field injection in undefined order
**Final fields**: Only constructor-injected dependencies can be marked final, ensuring immutability
**Avoid mixing all three**: While possible to add field injection to constructor plus setter, it creates inconsistency and reduces code clarity
**Testing benefit**: Mixing types doesn't compromise testability as long as required dependencies use constructor injection
**Production standard**: The constructor required plus setter optional pattern is widely adopted in enterprise Spring Boot applications

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Yes, a Spring bean can absolutely mix injection types. The common pattern is constructor injection for required dependencies and setter injection for optional ones. For example, imagine an OrderService. It needs an OrderRepository and a PaymentGateway to function, so those go in the constructor as final fields. But it can also use a CacheService to speed up queries if caching is configured. That one goes in a setter method marked with at-Autowired required equals false. Spring calls the constructor first, passing in the required dependencies. Then it looks for setter methods and field injection annotations and processes those. The order between setters and fields isn't guaranteed, but constructor always happens first. You can technically throw field injection into the mix too, but that defeats the purpose. If you've already got the constructor for required dependencies, adding at-Autowired on fields just makes your code inconsistent. The constructor plus setter combination gives you immutability for required dependencies and flexibility for optional ones. Most production Spring Boot apps follow this pattern. The common mistake freshers make is thinking you have to pick one injection type for the whole class. You don't. You use the right type for each dependency based on whether it's required or optional. That's the pragmatic approach in real projects.

question: What is the problem with field injection and unit testing?
title: Field Injection and Unit Testing Problem
direct_answer: **Field injection breaks unit testing** without Spring. Since `@Autowired` fields are private and injected via reflection, you cannot set them with `new MyService(mockRepo)`. You need the Spring context or reflection hacks like `ReflectionTestUtils.setField()` to test, making tests slow and complex.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical testing knowledge and why DI type matters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not understanding why field injection makes testing harder
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast: 3 lines to test with constructor injection vs needing @SpringBootTest or ReflectionTestUtils with field injection

sections.title: Why Field Injection Kills Unit Test Simplicity
sections.content: Field injection creates a serious testing problem: **you cannot instantiate the class outside of Spring's control**. Since `@Autowired` fields are private and set via reflection, there's no public way to pass in a mock dependency. With constructor injection, you write `new OrderService(mockRepository)` and you're done — a pure unit test with no framework. With field injection, you have two bad choices: (1) Start the entire Spring application context using `@SpringBootTest`, which loads all beans, connects to databases, and runs for seconds instead of milliseconds. (2) Use `ReflectionTestUtils.setField(service, "orderRepo", mockRepo)` to bypass Java's access rules and force the dependency in — brittle, verbose, and error-prone. Both approaches slow down test suites and add complexity. In a large codebase with hundreds of services, field injection can make unit tests 100x slower than necessary.

sections.title: Testing Constructor vs Field Injection
Key Points
content: **Private field problem**: @Autowired fields are private, so you can't set them from test code using normal Java
**Constructor injection testing**: Clean 3-line test with new MyService(mockDependency), no Spring framework needed
**@SpringBootTest cost**: Starts full application context, loads all beans, connects to databases, runs 100x slower than pure unit tests
**ReflectionTestUtils hack**: Spring's utility to set private fields in tests, but it's brittle and breaks refactoring
**Test suite impact**: In a project with 500 service classes, field injection can add hours to full test suite runtime
**Mocking frameworks**: Both Mockito and constructor injection work together easily, but field injection requires Spring's @MockBean
**Production consequence**: Teams often skip unit tests entirely for field-injected classes and only write integration tests, losing fast feedback

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The problem with field injection and unit testing is that you can't instantiate the class without Spring. When you use at-Autowired on a private field, Spring sets that field using reflection. But in a test, you can't just call new OrderService and pass in a mock repository because there's no constructor parameter for it. The field is private, so you can't set it directly either. You have two options, both bad. Option one is to use at-SpringBootTest. That starts the entire Spring application context just to test one service class. It loads all your beans, connects to the database, and takes seconds to run. Compare that to a pure unit test with constructor injection, which runs in milliseconds. Option two is to use ReflectionTestUtils dot setField. That's a Spring utility that forces the value into the private field using reflection. It works, but it's brittle. If you rename the field, your test breaks. And it's verbose, adding three extra lines per dependency. With constructor injection, you just write new OrderService with a mock repo, and you're done. Three lines total. The test is fast because there's no Spring context. It's clear because the constructor shows exactly what the service needs. And it's refactor-safe because the compiler catches mistakes. The real-world impact in a large codebase is huge. If you have 500 service classes all using field injection, running your full test suite can take hours instead of minutes. That's why production teams strongly prefer constructor injection.

If you want to inject a mock into a field-injected dependency, you either need Spring to do it (slow) or use a reflection utility (fragile). Constructor injection has no such problem — you just pass the mock as a constructor argument.

Unit tests should be fast, isolated, and simple. @SpringBootTest loads the entire application context — it takes 10 to 30 seconds per test class. ReflectionTestUtils.setField() is a string-based reflection hack that breaks silently when you rename the field. Neither is acceptable for a codebase with hundreds of tests.

@SpringBootTest workaround: loads the full Spring context. Works but takes seconds — unacceptable for unit tests.
ReflectionTestUtils.setField() workaround: sets private fields via Spring's reflection utility. Fragile — renaming the field silently breaks the test.
@InjectMocks (Mockito): tries to inject mocks into annotated fields via reflection. Brittle and non-transparent.
Constructor injection solution: new UserService(mock(UserRepository.class)) — three lines, zero Spring, runs in milliseconds.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, UserService uses constructor injection. The test class has exactly three lines of setup: UserRepository mockRepo = mock(UserRepository.class); UserService svc = new UserService(mockRepo); when(mockRepo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(testUser));. No annotations, no context loading, no reflection hacks. sharp edge: a project with 500 test classes where each uses @SpringBootTest adds 5,000 to 15,000 seconds to the CI pipeline. Constructor injection eliminates that overhead entirely.

items: Don't use @InjectMocks as a substitute for constructor injection — it uses reflection under the hood and breaks on field rename just like ReflectionTestUtils.
Don't accept slow tests as unavoidable — if your test needs @SpringBootTest just to set a field, that's a design problem, not a Spring limitation.

question: Does Spring Boot require @Autowired for constructor injection?
title: @Autowired Required for Constructor Injection in Spring Boot
direct_answer: **No.** Since Spring 4.3, if a class has only one constructor, Spring automatically uses it for injection without needing `@Autowired`. Spring Boot takes advantage of this — you just define the constructor with the dependencies as parameters and Spring wires them.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor as idiomatic modern Spring Boot code

sections.title: Spring's Implicit Constructor Injection
sections.content: Since **Spring Framework 4.3** (released in 2016), the `@Autowired` annotation on constructors became optional when a class has exactly one constructor. Spring Boot, which builds on Spring Framework, inherits this behavior. This **implicit constructor injection** is Spring's convention-over-configuration principle at work: if there's only one constructor, Spring assumes you want that constructor used for dependency injection. The feature eliminates boilerplate without sacrificing clarity — the constructor signature still explicitly lists all dependencies. If your class has multiple constructors, you must mark one with `@Autowired` to tell Spring which one to use. But in the common case of a service with one constructor taking its repository dependencies, you just write the constructor and Spring wires it automatically. Modern Spring Boot code rarely has `@Autowired` on constructors because most services follow this single-constructor pattern.

sections.title: Constructor Injection Without @Autowired
Key Points
content: **Spring 4.3 feature**: @Autowired on constructors is optional when the class has exactly one constructor
**Spring Boot default**: All Spring Boot versions use this implicit constructor injection behavior
**Single constructor rule**: If there's one constructor, Spring uses it automatically; multiple constructors require explicit @Autowired
**Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor**: Generates a constructor for all final fields, combining with implicit injection for zero DI boilerplate
**Clarity preservation**: Removing @Autowired doesn't hide dependencies; they're still explicit in the constructor parameters
**Legacy code**: Older Spring applications pre-4.3 will have @Autowired on every constructor, but it's not needed in modern code
**Best practice**: Modern Spring Boot style is final fields plus Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor for cleanest dependency injection

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: No, Spring Boot doesn't require at-Autowired for constructor injection. Since Spring Framework version 4.3, if your class has only one constructor, Spring automatically uses that constructor for dependency injection. You don't need any annotation. Spring Boot builds on top of Spring Framework, so it inherits this behavior. You just write a constructor with your dependencies as parameters, and Spring wires them up at runtime. For example, if your OrderService has one constructor taking an OrderRepository, Spring sees that single constructor and says okay, I'll use this one for injection. The dependencies are still explicit in the constructor signature, so you haven't hidden anything. If your class has multiple constructors, then you do need at-Autowired on one of them to tell Spring which constructor to use. But most services follow a pattern of one constructor with all their required dependencies, so you rarely see at-Autowired in modern Spring Boot code. There's an even cleaner approach using Lombok. The at-RequiredArgsConstructor annotation generates a constructor for all final fields at compile time. Combine that with Spring's implicit constructor injection, and you get zero boilerplate. Just mark your dependencies as final, add at-RequiredArgsConstructor to the class, and you're done. Spring wires everything automatically. That's the idiomatic style in modern Spring Boot applications. The common mistake is adding at-Autowired on every constructor because that's what older tutorials show. It's not wrong, but it's unnecessary noise in new code.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring 4.3 quietly made @Autowired optional on constructors — modern Spring Boot code has no @Autowired anywhere.

beats.text: Since Spring 4.3, if a class has exactly one constructor, Spring uses it automatically for dependency injection without requiring @Autowired. Spring detects the single constructor, resolves its parameters from the container, and calls it. You only need @Autowired when the class has multiple constructors and you need to tell Spring which one to use.
The @Autowired on constructors was always redundant when there was only one option. Spring 4.3 cleaned that up. The result is cleaner code — less annotation noise, more signal.

items: Single constructor: Spring uses it automatically. No @Autowired needed.
Multiple constructors with one @Autowired: Spring uses the annotated one.
Multiple constructors with no @Autowired: Spring falls back to the no-arg constructor. If there isn't one, it throws NoSuchMethodException.
Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor: generates a constructor for all final fields. Combine with @Service and you have clean, annotation-light Spring Boot code.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, UserService is annotated @Service and @RequiredArgsConstructor. It has private final UserRepository repo and private final EmailService emailSvc. Lombok generates the two-parameter constructor. Spring sees the single constructor and injects both beans. The class has no @Autowired anywhere — it's completely clean. non-obvious: @RequiredArgsConstructor only generates constructors for final and @NonNull fields. If you have a non-final field in the class, it won't be included in the constructor.

items: If you add a second constructor without @Autowired, Spring falls back to the no-arg constructor — if that doesn't exist, startup fails with a confusing error.
Don't mix @RequiredArgsConstructor with manually written constructors — they may conflict and confuse Spring.

speakable_v2.cap: The idiomatic modern Spring Boot service has @Service, @RequiredArgsConstructor, and final fields — no @Autowired, no constructor body, full DI benefits.
